doc.title: Wayne Andre interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

chapter: Childhood, Berklee and the Air Force
title: Air Force arrangements and Sammy Nestico
summary: The warrant officer tried to keep his arrangements; Andre took them. He says he never considered a service career like Nestico.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: It’s like having a baby. When I was in the service I’d just finished writing or copying an arrangement when I had come down the next morning we’d have jazz band and I’d put it down, let’s do it. You know what I’m saying? I did a lot of writing in the service. I remember the Warrant Officer, who was in charge of the band, subsequently went on and became Colonel Gabriel, the head of all the Air Force bands in Washington, after I left he went down to Washington. As I was getting out of the service he tried to stop me from taking my arrangements. And I had to go above his head and say this was not my CO, or whatever you call it, I forget what it was. This is not — I’m here as a trombone player. So if I did this writing I did it on my own time. I didn’t do it on Air Force time so it doesn’t belong to the Air Force, so I ended up taking all my arrangements. He wanted to keep them. Because he had started a little band or something and he wanted to keep all that music.
It must have been pretty good then.
But I didn’t have much money so I sat around the barracks and I was writing music.
Did you ever consider making a career out of the service?

No. No. I mean Sammy Nestico did and I think Sammy Nestico has had a fantastic life. He stayed in the service twenty years. He went in very young and he came out and he just like blossomed. And so twenty years lost, if you think of it as lost in the service, for Sammy Nestico, they were really not lost, I mean he had a good job in Washington and everything else. But you have to know Sammy Nestico.
